repot.description: Not applicable — landscape shrub.

subcategories.label: Powdery mildew
subcategories.description: White powdery coating on leaf surfaces during warm, humid weather — common in late summer at Church Mountain Road. Primarily cosmetic. Improve air circulation around the plant. Potassium bicarbonate or neem oil spray for control if severe. Avoid overhead watering.

subcategories.label: Botrytis blight
subcategories.description: Gray fuzzy mold on flowers and buds during cool, damp weather — spring and fall are peak windows at this elevation. Remove and dispose of affected flower heads. Improve air circulation. Fungicide treatment rarely needed in landscape settings.

subcategories.label: Late frost bud damage
subcategories.peakWindow: Apr–early May — critical watch period at ~2,959 ft elevation
subcategories.description: Old-wood flower buds are vulnerable to late spring frosts. Check the 10-day forecast in April and early May. When a hard frost (<28°F) is predicted, cover with frost cloth or old bedsheets overnight. Even with bud loss, the reblooming genetics ensure bloom on new wood later in the season.

bloom.note: A reblooming bigleaf — flowers on both old and new wood, so a late frost won't cost the whole show.

plants.name: Pop Star Endless Summer Reblooming Hydrangea
plants.guide: The Pop Star hydrangea is a compact reblooming bigleaf that produces abundant lacey blue or pink mophead flowers on both old and new wood from early summer through fall. The reblooming habit is the defining trait — even if a late spring frost damages old-wood flower buds, new buds develop and bloom through the growing season. Flower color is soil pH dependent: acidic soils (4.5–5.5) yield blue; alkaline soils (above 7.0) yield pink. At Church Mountain Road's native pH, expect blue flowers without amendment. Low-maintenance, pollinator magnet, electric color in the landscape.
plants.currentSeasonNote: Late May at Church Mountain Road — the plant is leafed out and flower buds are swelling. First bloom should emerge in 2–3 weeks (early-to-mid June at ~2,959 ft elevation, about a week later than valley plants). Check for emerging buds on old wood from last season. If any shoots show frost damage from a late freeze, do not cut them back — new buds will develop and bloom on new wood through summer. Keep consistently watered as active growth accelerates.
plants.soilNotes: Thrives in Hayesville/Cecil/Pacolet soils at Church Mountain Road. The native acidic pH (4.5–5.5) is ideal for blue flowers — no lime amendment needed. Bigleaf hydrangeas demand moist, well-drained soil rich in organic matter. Amend the planting hole generously with compost at establishment. Avoid low spots with standing water or heavy clay subsoil that stays wet in winter — root rot is the enemy. On flat areas at the property where clay Bt argillic subsoil impedes drainage, use a raised or bermed bed position.
plants.aspectPreference: Part sun to part shade. East-facing positions with morning sun and afternoon shade are ideal at Church Mountain Road — afternoon summer sun can scorch leaves and stress the plant, reducing bloom. North-facing exposures work but may reduce flowering by 20–30%. Avoid hot south or west exposures without supplemental irrigation during July–September dry stretches. The property's east-facing mid-slope positions are textbook hydrangea habitat.
plants.frostSensitivity: Hardy to Zone 4 overall, but old-wood flower buds are vulnerable to late spring frosts. At ~2,959 ft elevation, the May 1–21 window is the critical frost-risk period for buds on last year's growth — a real concern at Church Mountain Road. The reblooming genetics mean the plant will still flower on new wood even if old-wood buds are lost, but the first bloom flush may be delayed or reduced. Protect with frost cloth during late spring freeze events if possible, or site in the thermal belt mid-slope position where frost risk is slightly lower than in hollows.

prune.peakWindow: Mar — after last hard freeze, before bud swell
prune.description: Prune conservatively in late winter (Feb–early Mar, before bud swell). Remove only clearly dead wood (brown, dried stems with no live buds). Do not cut back healthy stems as they carry the first bloom buds. At Church Mountain Road elevation, last hard freeze typically occurs around mid-April, so hold off major pruning until late February to March to avoid hitting it. After the first bloom flush (late June–July), lightly deadhead spent flower clusters and remove any weak or crossing stems. Full renovation cuts (to near ground level) can be done in late winter every 3–4 years to rejuvenate old plants, accepting one season of reduced bloom.

propagate.description: Take 4–5 inch tip cuttings from non-flowering stems in early summer (Jun–Jul). Remove lower leaves, dip in rooting hormone, and stick in a perlite/peat mix. Keep shaded and consistently moist. Rooting takes 4–6 weeks. The Pop Star cultivar may be protected by plant patents — check before propagating for distribution.

fertilize.description: Apply a balanced slow-release fertilizer (e.g., 10-10-10 or azalea/rhododendron formulation) in early spring (Mar) as growth begins. A second lighter application in May before bloom promotes strong flower development. Avoid fertilizing after July — late-season nitrogen promotes soft growth more susceptible to frost damage. At Church Mountain Road's native soil pH, the azalea-specific formulations are ideal as they include micronutrients suited to acidic mountain soils.

water.description: Bigleaf hydrangeas are among the most moisture-demanding landscape shrubs. Water deeply 2–3 times per week during hot dry stretches (June–September). Morning watering is preferred; avoid wetting foliage in the evening. Mulch 2–3 inches around the base to retain moisture and keep roots cool. At Church Mountain Road, the cooler mountain climate and higher rainfall (estimated 62–68 in/yr at elevation) reduce stress compared to lowland sites, but supplemental water is still critical during the July–August dry window when afternoon thunderstorms can be sporadic.

repot.description: Not applicable — landscape shrub.

subcategories.label: Powdery mildew
subcategories.description: White powdery coating on leaf surfaces during warm humid weather — common in late summer at Church Mountain Road when RH climbs to 70–90%. Primarily cosmetic but worth managing. Improve air circulation around the plant. Potassium bicarbonate or neem oil spray for control if severe. Avoid overhead watering — wet foliage in evening promotes the disease.

subcategories.label: Botrytis blight
subcategories.description: Gray fuzzy mold on flowers and buds during cool, damp weather — spring (March–April) and fall (September–October) are peak windows at this elevation. Remove and dispose of affected flower heads. Improve air circulation. Fungicide treatment rarely needed in landscape settings.

subcategories.label: Late frost old-wood bud damage
subcategories.peakWindow: Apr–early May — critical watch period at ~2,959 ft elevation
subcategories.description: Old-wood flower buds are vulnerable to late spring frosts. At Church Mountain Road, check the 10-day forecast in April and early May. When a hard frost (<28°F) is predicted, consider covering with frost cloth or old bedsheets overnight. Even with old-wood bud loss, the reblooming genetics ensure strong bloom on new wood later in the season — this is the insurance policy built into the variety.

_phaseF.elevationFit: Excellent fit at 2,959 ft. Reblooming genetics mean late frost loss of old-wood buds won't prevent blooming. Cooler summer temps at elevation extend bloom season compared to lowland GA.
_phaseF.habitatHint: East-facing mid-slope with morning sun and afternoon shade. Avoid full south/west exposure without supplemental water.
_phaseF.fromCommonName: Endless Summer Pop Star Reblooming Hydrangea

bloom.note: Endless Summer type — reblooms continuously on new wood once established.

plants.name: Spiderwort
plants.guide: The spiderwort on the property is a native eastern wildflower at home in moist woodland edges and dappled shade — exactly the habitat Church Mountain Road offers. The three-petaled purple-blue flowers open in morning and close by afternoon, but the plant produces new buds continuously through late spring and early summer. Extremely low-maintenance once established; spreads by self-seeding and underground rhizomes. Totally harmless to wildlife and pets. The common name references the spidery quality of the stamens and the thread-like leaf bases.
plants.currentSeasonNote: Late May at Church Mountain Road — peak bloom time. The plant flowers most prolifically in cool moist spring weather; as temperatures rise and daylength increases through June, bloom slows (the flowers are sensitive to heat and bright afternoon sun). Right now is prime time to enjoy the display. Deadheading spent flowers extends bloom, but spiderwort self-seeds readily if you leave flowers to mature — both approaches work.
plants.soilNotes: Ideally suited to Church Mountain Road's Hayesville/Cecil/Pacolet soils. Prefers moist, well-drained loam rich in organic matter at pH 5.5–7.0 — the native slightly acidic (4.5–5.5) mountain soils are acceptable, especially when amended with compost or leaf mulch. Tolerates seasonal wet feet better than many woodland plants but despises permanently waterlogged clay subsoil. Established plants are reasonably drought-tolerant once their rhizomes are deep, but spring through early summer moisture (when actively flowering and setting seed) is critical for the best display.
plants.aspectPreference: Partial shade to dappled sun — north and east-facing woodland edges are ideal at Church Mountain Road. Morning sun with afternoon shade from the forest canopy is the sweet spot. Too much afternoon heat and bright sun causes the flowers to wilt and close early in the day. Full shade reduces flowering significantly. The moist woodland edge habitat at this elevation is perfect — the plant does not thrive in hot, dry, full-sun locations even with irrigation.
plants.frostSensitivity: Hardy USDA Zone 3 — extremely cold-tolerant. No frost concerns at Church Mountain Road elevation. The foliage emerges in late April at ~2,959 ft (about 1–2 weeks later than lowland Georgia) and can handle a late frost without damage. The emerging shoots are soft and bright green but recover quickly from frost. Established rhizomes are completely frost-proof and persist through winter.

prune.peakWindow: May 20–Jun 15 — as first flush of flowers begins to fade
prune.description: Deadheading extends bloom significantly — remove spent flowers just below the flower head on the stem to prevent seed formation and redirect energy into new bud development. At Church Mountain Road elevation, deadheading through early June maintains peak flowering. After late June as temperatures rise and daylength peaks, deadheading becomes less critical and the plant's energy naturally shifts toward seed production and vegetative growth. Optional: cut back the entire plant (stems and foliage) to 6 inches after the main bloom window ends in mid-to-late June — this encourages fresh new growth and sometimes produces a secondary lighter bloom flush in late summer or early fall.

propagate.peakWindow: Sep–Oct seed collection; early spring division
propagate.description: Two methods: (1) Division — in early spring (Mar–Apr) before active growth or in fall (Aug–Sep) after bloom, carefully dig and separate the rhizome-connected plantlets. Each piece with roots and a fan of leaves will establish quickly if replanted immediately at the same depth and kept consistently moist for the first season. (2) Seed — let mature seedpods dry on the plant through summer; collect in September–October and direct-sow in a prepared bed or cold frame. Seed germinates readily without stratification if given moisture and cool nights (fall sowing is most reliable). Seedlings appear in spring and reach flowering size in 1–2 years. The property's native soil supports self-seeding naturally — volunteers often appear nearby if you leave flowers unmulched.

fertilize.peakWindow: Mar–Apr before active growth; May–early Jun before peak bloom
fertilize.description: Light hand. Early spring (Mar–Apr) with a balanced slow-release fertilizer (e.g., Plant-tone or 10-10-10) awakens the plant after dormancy. A second light application in late April–early May supports robust flowering. Church Mountain Road's naturally organic-matter-rich soil and annual leaf mulch additions usually provide sufficient nutrition — over-fertilizing produces lush foliage at the expense of flowers and promotes weak growth susceptible to fungal disease in humid conditions. If plants are yellowing or obviously stunted, a soil test through UGA Extension is worth the $9.

water.description: Critical April through early July when actively flowering and setting seed. Deep soaking once a week beats daily light watering — the goal is moist but not waterlogged soil. At Church Mountain Road's estimated 62–68 in/yr precipitation (valley baseline 57 in plus 5–15% orographic lift), established plants in good drainage rarely need supplemental summer water except during drought stretches. Spring through early June is the priority window — consistent moisture at this time ensures peak bloom and good seed set. Apply 2–3 inches of leaf-litter mulch year-round to retain moisture and moderate soil temperature.

repot.description: Not applicable — spiderwort is a landscape perennial, not a container plant.

inspect.description: Generally pest- and disease-free. In very humid summers (Church Mountain Road's 70–90% summer RH), watch for leaf spot diseases or occasional powdery mildew on lower foliage — mostly cosmetic. Improve air circulation by removing lower spent leaves and avoiding overhead watering. The plant is rarely bothered by insects. If slugs damage the emerging foliage in spring, apply iron-phosphate bait (Sluggo) around the base in April.

_phaseF.elevationFit: Native to eastern deciduous forest; very plausible at 2,959 ft in moist woodland edges
_phaseF.habitatHint: Moist woodland edges, part shade, self-seeding

bloom.note: Each flower lasts a morning; the plant opens fresh ones for weeks.

plants.name: Creeping Fig
plants.guide: Creeping fig is a tender evergreen climbing fig — small, leathery heart-shaped leaves on wiry stems that cling to walls and supports by aerial rootlets. By the book it's only reliably hardy to about Zone 8, so at 2,959 ft you'd expect it to be a tender seasonal here — but ours has proven otherwise. The plant on the property came through the winter outdoors and leafed back out the following spring (Mom noticed it returning in spring 2026), so on its sheltered footing it's earning a permanent spot rather than living as a one-season annual. Give it part shade and steady moisture through the warm months and it flushes happily. Help it through the cold — a deep mulch over the roots and a cover on the hardest nights — and there's good reason to expect it back each spring. Taking a few cuttings in late summer is still worth doing as cheap insurance.
plants.currentSeasonNote: June: in full warm-season growth — the good stretch. Keep it evenly watered and let it run. Ours came through last winter outdoors, so the job now isn't to brace for losing it but to keep it thriving: water through the summer, then mulch the roots deep before the first frosts and drape a cover over it on the hardest nights. A few late-summer cuttings make a nice backup.
plants.soilNotes: Wants moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil and does NOT like to dry out — the opposite of the property's drought-tolerant natives like the butterfly weed. The native Hayesville/Cecil/Pacolet acidic loams suit it fine as long as moisture stays steady; mulch to hold water. In a container, use a rich potting mix that still drains freely.
plants.aspectPreference: Part shade to filtered sun. Protect it from harsh afternoon sun and drying wind — a sheltered east-facing wall or a spot under high shade gives it the best summer. Deep shade slows it; blazing exposure scorches the thin leaves.
plants.frostSensitivity: Tender by the book — reliably hardy only to about Zone 8 on paper, with foliage that can take damage in the upper 20s°F. At 2,959 ft in Zone 6b that would normally make it a gamble outdoors, but the plant here has already proven it can take a winter on this property: it came back in spring 2026 after the previous winter. Treat it as tender-but-established rather than doomed, and give it the help that keeps it that way — a deep mulch (4–6 in) mounded over the roots and crown before hard cold sets in, and a frost cloth, old sheet, or cardboard draped over the top growth on the coldest nights (single digits / hard sustained freezes). A sheltered, out-of-the-wind footing against a wall is what tips the odds its way here. A few late-summer cuttings are still worth taking as insurance, but on current evidence this one earns a permanent place.

prune.description: Pinch and trim during active warm-season growth to encourage branching and keep it tidy on its support. It's vigorous when warm, so light, frequent tip-pinching beats one hard cut. Hold off in the cold months — let it rest, and wait until spring growth resumes to clean up any winter-burned tips rather than cutting them off in fall.

subcategories.label: Stem cuttings (overwintering)
subcategories.peakWindow: Aug–early Sep, well before first frost
subcategories.description: Cheap insurance rather than a necessity, now that the outdoor plant has wintered over here. Take 3–5 inch stem cuttings in late summer, before frost — they root very easily, in water or a moist, free-draining mix. Pot up the rooted cuttings and overwinter them on a bright indoor windowsill as a backup, then plant out after the May frost date if you want to spread it to a new spot.

fertilize.description: Light feeding during the active warm season supports the summer flush — a balanced liquid feed every few weeks is plenty. Ease off by late summer so you're not pushing soft growth right as you take cuttings. No feeding outdoors in the cold months.

water.description: Keep evenly moist all through the warm season — creeping fig does not tolerate drying out, and the thin leaves wilt fast in heat. Water more in hot, dry spells and mulch around the roots to hold moisture. Container plants dry out quickest — check them often.

repot.description: Only relevant if you're growing it in a pot to lift in and out. Refresh or step up the pot in early spring as the overwintered plant comes back into growth, before setting it outside after the frost date.

subcategories.label: Winter protection
subcategories.peakWindow: mid Oct–Nov — get protection on before hard cold
subcategories.description: Not a pest watch — this is about helping it through the cold. Our plant has wintered over outdoors here, and the way to keep it doing so is to get protection on before the hard freezes: mound 4–6 inches of mulch over the roots and crown in mid-to-late autumn, and keep a frost cloth or sheet handy to drape over the top growth on the coldest nights. If the top does burn back in a brutal winter, don't pull it — wait for spring and it may well push fresh growth from the protected crown.

subcategories.label: Indoor pests (if overwintered)
subcategories.description: Only relevant if you're keeping cuttings or a potted backup indoors over winter. Indoors, creeping fig is prone to the usual dry-air houseplant pests — scale, mealybug, and especially spider mites in heated rooms. Keep humidity up, check leaf undersides, and treat early with insecticidal soap.

plants.name: Fairway Turf
plants.guide: The mowed fairway below the house is the one piece of ground here run as turf rather than meadow — kept green, even, and close-cut. Turf-type tall fescue is the grass for it: a cool-season bunchgrass that's the standard choice for North Georgia lawns and an even better fit at this elevation, where the summers run too cool for Bermuda and far too humid for the creeping bentgrass a golf course would use. (The “autumn bentgrass” Mom flagged is a different plant entirely — a native meadow grass, not a turf.) Fescue grows in clumps rather than running, so it never knits over bare spots on its own; the fairway stays lush because the thin places get overseeded every fall, not because any one season is allowed to slide.
plants.currentSeasonNote: Right now — late spring is peak fescue growth. Mow tall and often (3–3.5″) and leave the clippings. Hold the nitrogen: feeding now drives soft blades straight into summer brown-patch weather. Mark the thin or bare spots you notice — September is the month to fix them.
plants.soilNotes: Native ground here is acidic (pH 4.5–5.5); fescue wants 6.0–6.5, so a fall application of dolomitic lime — sized to a UGA soil test, not guessed — is the single biggest lever on turf color. The Hayesville/Cecil/Pacolet loams drain well on the slope. Retest every three years.
plants.aspectPreference: Full sun on the open, south-facing clearing — ideal light for fescue. The same exposure that melts frost and greens the fairway first in spring also dries it fastest in a summer drought, so summer water lands here before anywhere else on the property.
plants.frostSensitivity: Cool-season grass: greens up early, holds color late, and shrugs off light frost and snow. Its hard season is summer, not winter — deep heat and humidity, not cold, are what stress it. Hardy well past the property's Zone 6b winters.

mow.description: Mow high — 3 to 3.5 inches — and never take off more than a third of the blade in one pass. Tall fescue holds color and crowds out weeds when it's cut tall; scalp it and you invite crabgrass and disease. Raise the deck to 3.5–4″ through the June–August heat so the longer blades shade the roots and slow brown patch. Leave the clippings — they return free nitrogen. Keep the mower blade sharp; a torn tip browns and stresses the plant.

propagate.peakWindow: Sep 1–25 — the one window that matters
propagate.description: Tall fescue is a bunchgrass — it grows in clumps and won't spread to fill bare spots on its own, so the fairway stays full only if you overseed thin areas every fall. September beats spring by far: the seed roots through two cool seasons before it ever faces summer. Rake or scratch the soil, sow turf-type tall fescue seed (about 5–6 lb per 1,000 sq ft on bare ground, 3–4 to thicken existing turf), and keep the top inch moist until it germinates in one to two weeks. Avoid spring seeding — young fescue rarely survives its first mountain summer.

subcategories.label: Fall feeding
subcategories.description: Fall is when fescue does its real growing, and where almost all the year's nitrogen belongs. Feed once in mid-September as it wakes from summer, and again in early November to build roots for winter. A UGA soil test sizes the rate; in general, a slow-release lawn fertilizer at the label rate. Never push heavy nitrogen in spring or summer — it forces soft growth straight into brown-patch weather.

subcategories.label: Lime (soil-test driven)
subcategories.description: Native ground here runs acidic (pH 4.5–5.5); fescue wants 6.0–6.5. Dolomitic lime is slow to react, so a fall application gets the whole winter to work. Size it to a UGA Extension soil test (Pickens County, 706-253-8840, ~$9) rather than guessing — over-liming is as bad as none. Retest every three years.

subcategories.label: Light spring green-up
subcategories.description: At most a light feeding in March to green it up. Keep it modest — the fall feedings do the heavy lifting, and spring nitrogen mostly fuels disease and extra mowing.

subcategories.label: Summer survival
subcategories.description: In a dry mountain summer, water deeply and infrequently — about one inch a week including rain, in the early morning so the blades dry before night and dodge disease. The open south-facing fairway dries fastest of any ground on the property. Established fescue can also be left to go semi-dormant and brown in drought; it greens back up with the fall rains.

subcategories.label: New-seeding establishment
subcategories.description: Fresh September seed is the exception to deep-and-infrequent: keep the top inch of soil moist with short, frequent waterings until the seedlings are up and rooted — roughly two to three weeks — then taper back to the normal weekly soak.

subcategories.label: Brown patch watch
subcategories.description: Brown patch is fescue's main trouble here — roughly circular patches of tan, collapsed blades that appear in hot, humid stretches, worst where the lawn stays wet overnight. Manage it culturally first: water in the morning not the evening, raise the mowing height, hold off nitrogen, and improve airflow. Reach for a fungicide only if an outbreak is severe and spreading.

subcategories.label: Weeds
subcategories.description: The key pre-emergent timing is for crabgrass — put it down before the soil warms through the mid-50s°F, which at this elevation runs late February into March (about when the forsythia blooms). Spot-treat broadleaf weeds in fall, when they're easiest to knock back and the fescue is growing strongly enough to fill in behind them.

plants.name: Fairway Meadow
plants.guide: Beyond the mowed turf, the rest of the clearing is run the opposite way — as meadow. It's cut back hard just once a year and otherwise left to grow tall and loose. This is where the native warm-season bunchgrasses belong: little bluestem, switchgrass, indiangrass, and the autumn bentgrass Mom flagged for the property, threaded through with wildflowers. The contrast is the whole point — a crisp, close-mown fairway reading against a tall, seed-headed, pollinator-fed meadow. It also asks almost nothing in return: no lime, no fertilizer, no weekly mowing.
plants.currentSeasonNote: Right now — the meadow is coming up for the season. Leave it be: the warm-season grasses and wildflowers do their work straight through summer and into fall, feeding pollinators and setting seed. The only cut that matters comes next February.
plants.soilNotes: Leave it acidic and unlimed — the native grasses and wildflowers are adapted to the property's natural pH (4.5–5.5). No fertilizer: feeding a meadow favors weeds and floppy, lodging growth over the wildflowers you actually want.
plants.aspectPreference: Full sun, the same south-facing clearing as the turf — warm-season natives thrive in it. Drier upland spots suit little bluestem and indiangrass; the damp lower edge toward the spring drainage suits switchgrass and the autumn bentgrass.
plants.frostSensitivity: Warm-season grasses — they green late in spring and go dormant gold after fall frost, which is exactly the look you want. The standing dead growth gives winter structure and cover until the late-winter cut.

mow.peakWindow: Late Feb — one cut, before green-up
mow.description: Mow once a year in late winter, down to about 4–6 inches — never lower — to clear the previous season's dead growth before the new one starts and before ground-nesting birds get going. That single cut is the whole maintenance rhythm. The exception is establishment: in the first year of a newly seeded meadow, mow every 4–6 weeks at that same height through the season to hold back annual weeds while the slow native perennials root in, then drop to the once-a-year cut from year two on.

plants.name: Lizard's Tail
plants.guide: Lizard's Tail is a native wetland perennial of the southeastern US, typically found in shallow water or moist soil at pond and stream margins. The plant produces heart-shaped leaves and distinctive nodding white flower spikes that give it the common name. At Church Mountain Road, it is planted in soil adjacent to the pond rather than in standing water — a drier siting than its native habitat, though the proximity to the water table keeps it consistently moist.
plants.currentSeasonNote: July 2026: the plant is actively growing and spreading in its pond-adjacent location. Flower spikes likely emerging or recently emerged given the timing. The first full season at this site means phenology here is still being established — check again next July to confirm bloom timing at ~2,959 ft elevation.
plants.soilNotes: Saururus cernuus is native to swamp margins and shallow water but thrives in moist soil away from standing water. Church Mountain Road's Hayesville/Cecil soils in the pond-adjacent bed — acidic sandy loam to loam at pH 4.5–5.5 — are well-matched if the soil stays consistently moist through summer. The plant's shallow root system demands organic matter; mulch 2–3 inches with leaf litter or compost. Avoid any spot where drainage is so perfect the soil dries in summer heat.
plants.aspectPreference: Part shade to full shade. Saururus is native to the dappled understory of bottomland hardwood forests — the pond-margin setting here, especially if it receives morning light and afternoon shade from surrounding trees, is ideal. Direct hot afternoon sun will stress the plant unless soil moisture is absolutely consistent.
plants.frostSensitivity: Hardy to Zone 4. No frost concerns at Church Mountain Road elevation. The above-ground foliage dies completely to the ground after first hard frost (typically October–November at ~2,959 ft); the rhizome survives dormant in the soil and re-sprouts in spring.

prune.description: Cut back dead foliage after the first hard frost flattens the leaves. At Church Mountain Road elevation, this runs late October through November. Remove all above-ground growth down to the crown to tidy the pond edge and reduce overwintering pest habitat. Spring cleanup is also fine — either approach works. Do not cut back in fall and leave the dead stems; the plant prefers a clean cut-back.

propagate.description: Divide rhizomes in early spring (March–April) just as new shoots begin to emerge. Lift the entire clump, separate by hand into sections carrying 2–3 emerging buds and healthy roots, and replant immediately in moist soil. Alternatively, allow the plant to spread naturally — the rhizomes will creep through moist soil and fill the area over 2–3 seasons. This plant is self-spreading by rhizome in the right conditions.

fertilize.description: Light feeding in early spring (April) with a balanced slow-release fertilizer. Saururus evolved in rich organic bottomland soils — annual compost top-dressing (1–2 inches) is more valuable than synthetic fertilizer. Most established plants in consistently moist soil with decent organic matter need no supplemental feeding.

water.description: Consistent moisture is non-negotiable. At Church Mountain Road's pond-adjacent siting, the proximity to the water table likely keeps the plant satisfied through summer, but watch for any prolonged dry spell — if rainfall is light, deep watering once weekly in July–August is prudent. The shallow rhizome system dries quickly in full sun; afternoon shade helps reduce water stress.

repot.description: Not applicable — Saururus is a landscape perennial, not a container plant.

inspect.description: Monitor for signs of stress if any extended dry period occurs mid-summer. Wilting or yellowing foliage in July–August (when the plant should be vigorous) signals inadequate moisture. Check for slugs or other defoliating insects in damp pond-edge habitat — they are attracted to the moist soil. Lizard's Tail itself is quite pest-resistant; problems are usually cultural (drought or waterlogging).

bloom.note: Curved white flower spikes over the pond edge.

plants.name: Crocosmia
plants.scientificName: Crocosmia × crocosmiiflora (montbretia — possibly 'Lucifer'; confirm on the ground)
plants.guide: A summer torch — arching sprays of red-orange trumpets held over fans of sword-shaped leaves, opening mid-to-late summer just as the hydrangeas wind down. It grows from corms that multiply into clumps and naturalizes readily at this elevation. Hummingbirds work it hard. Wants full sun to light afternoon shade and, above all, well-drained ground.
plants.currentSeasonNote: In full bloom now at Church Mountain Road. Nothing to do mid-bloom but enjoy it — and cut a few stems for the vase if you like; they hold well. Keep it watered through a hot dry stretch.
plants.soilNotes: Fine in the property's acidic sandy loam, but drainage is the make-or-break: corms rot in soggy winter ground. A raised or sloped, free-draining spot is ideal.
plants.aspectPreference: Full sun gives the most flowers; a little afternoon shade is fine at elevation. Deep shade leaves it floppy and shy to bloom.
plants.frostSensitivity: Corms are hardy here (roughly to zone 5–6); the top dies back after frost and returns from the corm each spring. In a hard-winter year, a deep mulch over the clump is cheap insurance.

prune.description: Cut the foliage back once frost blackens it (late Oct–Nov), and tidy spent flower spikes through the season. Leave the corms in the ground.

propagate.description: Divide congested clumps every 3–4 years as growth begins in late winter/early spring: lift the chains of corms, separate, and replant the plump top corms. Near-effortless — this is how a single clump becomes a drift.

fertilize.description: A light feed as shoots emerge in spring is plenty; it's not a hungry plant. Go easy on nitrogen or you'll get leaves at the expense of flowers.

water.description: Water through the summer bloom in dry spells. Established clumps are fairly drought-tolerant once the show is over.

repot.description: Not applicable in the ground. Keep an eye that it doesn't overrun neighbors — it spreads.

subcategories.label: Spread / crowding
subcategories.description: Crocosmia naturalizes vigorously. If it starts crowding neighbors, lift and thin the corm chains in spring — the same job as dividing.

subcategories.label: Spider mites
subcategories.description: Hot, dry spells can bring spider mites — fine webbing and pale stippling on the blade-leaves. Hose off forcefully; rarely serious.

bloom.note: Seen in full bloom on the property in mid-July 2026.

plants.name: Garden Phlox
plants.guide: Tall garden phlox — domed clusters of pink-to-lavender and white flowers on upright stems through mid-to-late summer, sweetly fragrant and a magnet for butterflies and hummingbird moths. A dependable old-garden perennial here. Its one recurring nuisance is powdery mildew in humid stretches, so the whole game is giving it air and watering low.
plants.currentSeasonNote: In bloom now — and carrying some powdery mildew this year (the pale, dusty film on the leaves). It's mostly cosmetic: thin any crowded stems for airflow, water at the roots rather than overhead, and deadhead the spent trusses to coax a second flush.
plants.soilNotes: Happiest in richer, moisture-retentive soil — work compost in and keep it mulched to hold the roots cool and damp. The property's acidic loam suits it.
plants.aspectPreference: Full sun to light shade. Morning sun with good air movement is the mildew-beating combination; avoid still, damp, crowded corners, which is exactly where mildew takes hold.
plants.frostSensitivity: Fully hardy here (to about zone 4). It dies to the ground in winter and returns from the crown each spring.

subcategories.label: Spring thinning (for airflow)
subcategories.peakWindow: Late Mar–Apr as shoots reach ~6 in
subcategories.description: When the clump is a few inches up, remove about a third of the weakest stems at the base. Fewer, better-spaced stems mean far better air movement — the single most effective thing you can do against powdery mildew.

subcategories.label: Fall cutback
subcategories.description: After frost, cut the stems to the ground and clear the debris away (don't compost mildewed foliage — it re-seeds the problem next year).

propagate.description: Divide the clump every 3–4 years in early spring or early fall to keep it vigorous — lift and split the crown, replant the strong outer pieces. Basal cuttings in spring also root easily.

fertilize.description: Feed in early spring with a balanced slow-release and top-dress with compost; a second light feed in June supports the big bloom. Don't overdo nitrogen — soft, lush growth mildews worst.

water.description: Water deeply at the base in summer dry spells — steady moisture keeps it un-stressed and less mildew-prone. Never water overhead: wet leaves are how mildew spreads.

repot.description: Not applicable — a landscape perennial.

subcategories.label: Powdery mildew
subcategories.description: The recurring one, worse in Jasper's humid summers: a white powdery film on the leaves, seen on the property this year. Manage culturally first — thin for airflow, water low, deadhead, clear fallen leaves. Horticultural oil or a bicarbonate spray helps if severe; over time, favor mildew-resistant divisions.

subcategories.label: Spider mites
subcategories.description: Hot, dry stretches can bring spider mites (fine webbing, stippled leaves). Hose off; keeping the plant well-watered is the best prevention.

bloom.note: Seen blooming on the property in mid-July 2026.

plants.name: Panicle Hydrangea
plants.guide: The toughest and most sun-tolerant of the hydrangeas — a big upright shrub carrying elongated cone-shaped flower clusters that open lime-white in mid-summer and age to pink as fall comes on. Because it blooms on NEW wood, it's fully frost-safe and easy: cut it back hard in late winter for bigger heads. The property's specimen is a large, established shrub.
plants.currentSeasonNote: Coming into bloom now at Church Mountain Road — the cones are filling out lime-green to white in mid-July. Nothing to do but enjoy it; the color will deepen toward pink into September.
plants.soilNotes: The least fussy hydrangea for the property's acidic loam — tolerates a wider range than the bigleaf types. Soil pH does NOT change its color (that's a bigleaf-only trait). Compost annually.
plants.aspectPreference: Takes more sun than the bigleaf types — full sun to part shade both work at this elevation, and more sun means more and sturdier flower cones. The east and open exposures suit it well.
plants.frostSensitivity: Frost-safe. It blooms on the current season's growth, so it pushes new flower buds every spring regardless of winter cold or late frosts — the dependable bloomer of the group.

prune.description: Late winter (Feb–early Mar), before growth starts. Cut back hard to a strong low framework — the harder you cut, the bigger the flower heads (though fewer of them). It blooms on new wood, so this won't cost you any flowers.

propagate.description: Softwood tip cuttings in early summer root readily under a humidity dome in 3–4 weeks. Ground layering works too — pin a low branch to the soil and walk away.

fertilize.description: A balanced slow-release in early spring, optionally a second light feed in early June. Don't overfeed — floppy stems that can't hold the big cones are usually too much nitrogen.

water.description: Deep weekly watering through summer, especially while the cones are forming and opening. More drought-tolerant than the bigleaf types once established, but the flowers are better with steady moisture.

repot.description: Not applicable — a landscape shrub.

subcategories.label: Flopping / support
subcategories.description: Heavy flower cones after summer rain can pull branches down. If it flops, cut for the vase or lightly stake; over time a harder late-winter prune builds sturdier stems.

subcategories.label: Powdery mildew
subcategories.description: Less prone than the bigleaf types, but humid stretches can still bring a light powdery film. Mostly cosmetic; improve airflow if it recurs.

bloom.note: Opens lime-white and ages to pink; seen coming into bloom on the property in mid-July 2026.

_meta.habitatContext: South-facing fairway clearing on a forested mountain ridge. Mixed hardwood-pine forest (oak, hickory, white pine, mountain laurel). Adjacent to Lake Sequoyah (0.3 mi). Elevation suppresses some lowland species and attracts Blue Ridge montane specialists.
_meta.notes: Monthly presence ratings reflect typical patterns at ~2,959 ft in the North Georgia Blue Ridge. Actual timing shifts 1–2 weeks earlier in warm years. Spring arrival dates are approximate — watch eBird for real-time reports from Pickens/Dawson/Gilmer counties.

propertyHighlights.whyGoodBirding: Church Mountain Road sits at the edge of a south-facing fairway with forest on all sides — classic Blue Ridge edge habitat. The combination of open clearing, mature deciduous and pine forest, proximity to Lake Sequoyah, and elevation makes it a convergence zone for both montane specialists and woodland edge birds. Mornings after rain in May and early June are peak observation windows — warblers and thrushes are conspicuous.
topFeatures: South-facing fairway edge: attracts Indigo Bunting, Eastern Towhee, Scarlet Tanager on forested margins
Mature forest interior: Pileated Woodpecker, Wood Thrush, Ovenbird, Barred Owl
Lake Sequoyah proximity (0.3 mi): Belted Kingfisher, Great Blue Heron, Osprey in summer
Elevation 2,959 ft: Dark-eyed Juncos year-round, Blue Ridge breeding warblers, Rose-breasted Grosbeak
Hummingbird feeders (May–Sep): Ruby-throated Hummingbird visits daily during peak season

feederRecommendations.hummingbird: 1:4 sugar-water ratio, red feeder, hung May 1 — Sep 30. Clean every 3–5 days in summer heat. No red dye needed.
feederRecommendations.blackOilSunflower: Attracts Cardinals, Titmice, Chickadees, Nuthatches, Finches, Grosbeaks year-round. Hopper or platform feeder.
feederRecommendations.nyjer: Tube feeder for American Goldfinch, Pine Siskin (winter irruptions), and Purple Finch. Oct–Apr most productive.
feederRecommendations.suet: Year-round but especially important Oct–Mar. Attracts all woodpecker species, Brown Creeper, Carolina Wren.
feederRecommendations.platform: Scatter mixed millet and milo for Dark-eyed Juncos, White-throated Sparrows, and Eastern Towhees scratching on the ground.

species.name: Ruby-throated Hummingbird
species.habitat: Woodland edges, clearings, gardens with flowers
species.voice: High-pitched chipping; wings produce distinctive hum
species.notes: The most eagerly anticipated arrival of spring. Males arrive 1–2 weeks before females — expect the first male by late April at Church Mountain Road elevation. Hang feeders May 1. By July you may have 3–6 birds competing. The south-facing fairway with flower plantings is ideal foraging habitat. All depart by mid-October — take feeders in after a week of no activity.
species.feeder: 1:4 sugar-water in red feeder, clean every 3–5 days
species.funFact: The only hummingbird species that nests in eastern North America. Males perform a distinctive U-shaped dive display.

species.name: Scarlet Tanager
species.habitat: Mature deciduous forest, especially oak-dominated forest interior
species.voice: Robin-like song but burrier: 'queery-queery-queery.' Distinctive chip-burr call.
species.notes: One of North America's most striking birds — flaming red body with jet black wings. Almost exclusively in mature forest canopy, which makes it easy to hear and hard to see. At Church Mountain Road, look along the forested edges of the fairway and into the mature mixed forest. The 'chip-burr' call is the giveaway once you learn it. Males become olive-green in fall before departing.
species.feeder: Occasionally visits berry bushes; not a typical feeder bird
species.funFact: Often the most colorful songbird in the eastern forest, yet it spends most of its time in the treetops where its brilliant color blends with sun-dappled leaves.

species.name: Rose-breasted Grosbeak
species.habitat: Forest edges, woodland clearings, mixed hardwood forest
species.voice: Rich, melodious song — like a robin who had voice lessons. Sharp 'peek' call.
species.notes: Males are unmistakable: black and white with a brilliant rose-red triangle on the chest. Church Mountain Road's forest-edge habitat at elevation is prime territory. They're conspicuous at feeders during spring migration (May) and can be present as breeders through summer. The male's rich musical song is one of the highlights of a May morning on the property.
species.feeder: Enthusiastic feeder visitor — loves black-oil sunflower seeds. Platform or hopper feeder.
species.funFact: Both male and female sing, and the male shares incubation duties — unusual for a colorful songbird.

species.name: Indigo Bunting
species.habitat: Shrubby edges, briars, forest clearings, roadsides
species.voice: High, paired musical phrases — 'fire-fire, where-where, here-here.' Males sing persistently from treetops even at midday in summer.
species.notes: Males are dazzling electric blue — one of the most brilliant birds in North America. The south-facing fairway edge at Church Mountain Road is exactly the shrubby-edge habitat they prefer. Males sing persistently from utility lines and treetop perches. Females are plain brownish — easy to overlook. One of the most reliable summer breeders at this elevation.
species.feeder: Nyjer (thistle) seed and millet. May visit during migration.
species.funFact: Males navigate migration by the stars — young males memorize the rotation of the night sky in their first summer to use as a compass.

species.name: Wood Thrush
species.habitat: Moist mature deciduous forest with closed canopy and leaf litter
species.voice: Considered by many the most beautiful birdsong in North America: flute-like 'ee-o-lay' spiraling phrases, often heard at dawn and dusk. Can produce two notes simultaneously.
species.notes: The voice of the Blue Ridge forest in summer. Most active at dawn and dusk — the 'ee-o-lay' call from the deep woods is an iconic Church Mountain Road sound on May mornings. Nests in moist forest understory, foraging for worms in deep leaf litter. A species of conservation concern — forest fragmentation and cowbird parasitism have reduced populations significantly. Church Mountain Road's intact forest is high-quality breeding habitat.
species.feeder: Does not visit feeders — forages exclusively on the forest floor
species.funFact: Can produce two independent notes simultaneously, creating its ethereal sound. Listed as a species of high conservation concern — every intact mountain forest acre matters.

species.name: Pileated Woodpecker
species.habitat: Mature forest with large dead snags — essential for excavating carpenter ants
species.voice: Loud, crow-like laughing call: 'wuk-wuk-wuk-wuk.' Distinctive slow, resonant drumming.
species.notes: The largest woodpecker in North America — crow-sized, jet black with a flaming red crest. An unmistakable presence in any mature forest. Look for the distinctive rectangular excavation holes in standing dead trees — these are the calling card of the Pileated. The powerful blows while excavating for carpenter ants carry far through the woods. Church Mountain Road's mature mixed forest with standing dead snags is prime habitat. Once you hear its loud laughing call, you'll never forget it.
species.feeder: Suet feeders — especially cylinder suet cakes or suet logs hung vertically
species.funFact: Pileated woodpeckers excavate cavities large enough for Wood Ducks and other large cavity-nesters — they're keystone species for the forest ecosystem.

species.name: Barred Owl
species.habitat: Mature forest with large trees; often near water
species.voice: The classic 'who cooks for you, who cooks for you-all' — one of the most recognizable owl calls. Calling peaks in late winter (Jan–Mar) during courtship. Pairs will duet.
species.notes: The most common owl in the North Georgia mountains. Church Mountain Road's mature forest near Lake Sequoyah is ideal territory — Barred Owls prefer large trees near water. Most vocal Jan–Mar during breeding season. Calling often begins at dusk and may continue through the night. On quiet evenings, step outside and listen — you'll often hear them calling from the tree line. Occasionally calls during daylight hours, especially on overcast days.
species.feeder: Does not visit feeders — hunts small mammals, frogs, crayfish
species.funFact: Will respond to imitations of their call — carefully 'hooting' their pattern can sometimes bring them in close. They have no ear tufts (unlike Great Horned Owls) and their dark eyes distinguish them from most other owls.

species.name: Dark-eyed Junco
species.habitat: Forest edges, clearings, shrubby areas — widespread at elevation
species.voice: Simple musical trill. Smacking 'tick' call notes in flocks.
species.notes: The quintessential Blue Ridge mountain bird. While lowland Georgians see Juncos only in winter, Church Mountain Road at ~2,959 ft has breeding Juncos year-round. In winter the resident flock is joined by birds from higher elevations — you may have 20–40 birds scratching under feeders. The 'snowbird' is unmistakable: dark gray above, white below, with white outer tail feathers flashing in flight. One of the most consistent feeder birds on the property.
species.feeder: Scatter white millet and mixed seed on the ground or low platform feeder — they prefer to forage on the ground
species.funFact: One of the most studied songbirds in North America. At Church Mountain Road's elevation, these are year-round breeding residents — a privilege not available at lower elevations where they're winter-only visitors.

species.name: Eastern Towhee
species.habitat: Dense shrubby undergrowth, briars, forest edges with thick ground cover
species.voice: Classic 'drink-your-tea' song. 'Chewink' call — often you hear them before you see them scratching in leaf litter.
species.notes: A large, bold sparrow-relative with a striking black hood, rufous sides, and white belly. Almost exclusively in dense shrubby undergrowth — the briars and thick growth along the fairway edge are prime habitat. Males scratch noisily in leaf litter (kicking back with both feet simultaneously) and sing persistently from low perches. The 'drink-your-tea' phrase is one of the most characteristic sounds of a Carolina mountain spring morning.
species.feeder: Scratch mixed millet on the ground or low platform. Often forages directly under elevated feeders.
species.funFact: Their distinctive two-legged backward scratch in leaf litter is called 'double-scratching' — a technique for uncovering insects and seeds invisible to a single-foot scraper.

species.name: Wild Turkey
species.habitat: Mixed forest and open areas, forest edges — flocks forage broadly
species.voice: Males gobble loudly in spring. Hens cluck and yelp. Year-round soft clucking contact calls.
species.notes: Church Mountain Road and the surrounding Tate Mountain Estates area has excellent turkey habitat. Flocks of 5–20 birds regularly move across the property, especially in early morning and late afternoon. Spring (Mar–May) is peak activity as males gobble and display from the fairway. A tom in full strut on the fairway clearing in April is a spectacular sight. Hens nest in the forest understory — if you encounter a hen alone in May or June, she may be leading you away from a nest.
species.feeder: Cracked corn scattered on the ground. They will also forage under elevated feeders.
species.funFact: Wild Turkeys can run 25 mph and fly up to 55 mph in short bursts — they're far more agile than the domesticated birds suggest. Males can have a beard up to 12 inches long.

species.name: Broad-winged Hawk
species.habitat: Mature forest interior for breeding; ridgetops during fall migration
species.voice: Thin, high-pitched whistle: 'peeeee.' Easy to overlook — forest interior bird when breeding.
species.notes: A quiet forest hawk in summer that becomes one of the great spectacles of North American birding in fall. Broad-wingeds are the smallest and most numerous Buteo — they summer in Blue Ridge forests and then in mid-September, on northwest winds after a cold front, they stream south in spectacular 'kettles' of hundreds or thousands of birds. Church Mountain Ridge sits along the typical migration corridor — worth watching the sky on Sep 12–20 from the fairway on NW wind days for a chance to catch a kettle. Summer presence in the surrounding forest is plausible, but the thin 'peeeee' whistle is easy to miss — not yet confirmed at the property.
species.funFact: The September Broad-winged Hawk migration is one of the great wildlife spectacles of eastern North America. On peak days at Blue Ridge ridgetop watch sites, counts can exceed 10,000 birds in a single day.

species.name: Belted Kingfisher
species.habitat: Lake and stream edges — perches on branches or utility lines over water to dive-hunt
species.voice: Loud, rattling machine-gun call — unmistakable. Often heard before seen.
species.notes: Lake Sequoyah at 0.3 miles is the primary draw. The rattling call of a Kingfisher along the lake shore is a year-round sound. They perch on overhanging branches or any elevated spot over water, diving headfirst to catch fish. Females are more colorful than males (unusual for birds) — females have a rust-colored belly band in addition to the blue. Worth stopping at the lake specifically to watch them hunt.
species.feeder: Does not visit feeders — fish only
species.funFact: Unusually for birds, the female Belted Kingfisher is more colorful than the male, with a rust-colored belly band the male lacks.

species.name: Ovenbird
species.habitat: Mature deciduous forest floor with deep leaf litter
species.voice: Emphatic, escalating 'TEACHER-teacher-teacher-teacher-teacher' — one of the loudest and most distinctive calls of the summer forest.
species.notes: You'll hear this bird constantly on Church Mountain Road in May–June but rarely see it — it walks quietly on the forest floor under the leaf litter while its outsized voice rings through the woods. Named for the dome-shaped leaf-litter nest that resembles an outdoor oven. Church Mountain Road's mature deciduous forest is prime habitat. A warbler by classification, but behaves more like a thrush — walks rather than hops.
species.funFact: The Ovenbird builds its nest entirely on the forest floor, covered by a dome of leaves that makes it nearly invisible — the entrance faces away from the most likely disturbance direction.

species.name: Carolina Chickadee
species.habitat: Forest edges, woodland, gardens — one of the most adaptable species
species.voice: Clear whistled 'fee-bee-fee-bay' song. Distinctive 'chick-a-dee-dee-dee' call (more 'dee' notes = more alarm).
species.notes: The anchor species of any North Georgia feeder — the first bird to find a new feeder and the last to leave. Carolina Chickadees are central to mixed foraging flocks in fall and winter, often leading Tufted Titmice, Nuthatches, and Downy Woodpeckers through the forest. They cache seeds individually for winter retrieval. Cavity nesters — a small nest box (1.25 inch entrance hole) placed in a shrubby forest edge may attract breeding pairs.
species.feeder: Black-oil sunflower seeds. Will use any style of feeder.
species.funFact: The 'dee-dee-dee' call encodes real-time threat information — the more 'dee' notes, the more dangerous the predator. A small, agile predator like a Pygmy Owl gets far more 'dee' notes than a large, slow Red-tailed Hawk.

species.name: Great Blue Heron
species.habitat: Lake shores, stream edges, any shallow water
species.voice: Loud, prehistoric squawk when flushed. Silent when fishing.
species.notes: A regular presence at Lake Sequoyah. These large, slow-moving waders stand motionless in the shallows waiting for fish, then strike with lightning speed. Often seen flying between fishing spots — the slow, flap-flap-glide with neck kinked back is unmistakable. Will occasionally appear in any wet or boggy area near the property. Best observed from the Lake Sequoyah shoreline in early morning.
species.funFact: Despite its large size (up to 4.5 ft tall), the Great Blue Heron weighs only 5–6 pounds — its massive size is mostly feathers, hollow bones, and wingspan.

species.name: White-throated Sparrow
species.habitat: Dense shrubby areas, brush piles, forest edges — forages on the ground
species.voice: Pure whistled 'Old Sam Peabody Peabody Peabody' (or 'Oh sweet Canada Canada Canada') — one of the clearest, most beautiful winter bird songs.
species.notes: Common winter visitor to Church Mountain Road, often in loose flocks with Dark-eyed Juncos and Eastern Towhees scratching under feeders. Listen in winter for their clear, plaintive whistle from the brush piles and forest edges. They often begin singing on mild winter days in late February — a harbinger of spring approaching. Most depart for northern breeding grounds by late April.
species.feeder: Mixed millet and white millet scattered on the ground or low platform
species.funFact: White-throated Sparrows come in two color morphs — white-striped and tan-striped — and they almost always pair with the opposite morph. The reason this genetic polymorphism persists is one of ornithology's interesting puzzles.

Jan.watchFor: Barred Owls vocal on mild nights. Winter finch irruptions possible.

Feb.watchFor: First Eastern Bluebirds begin scouting nest boxes. Barred Owl pairs duetting.

Mar.watchFor: American Woodcock evening sky-dance display in clearing at dusk (first 30 min after sunset). Wild Turkey toms beginning to strut.

Apr.watchFor: Hang hummingbird feeders Apr 25. First wave of spring warblers in early April. Rose-breasted Grosbeak and Scarlet Tanager often arrive together in late April.

May.watchFor: Best birding month of the year. Walk the forest edge at dawn May 5–15. Indigo Bunting singing from treetops. Turkey hens likely nesting.

Jun.watchFor: Hummingbirds at peak. Wood Thrush and Ovenbird consistently audible at dawn. Ruby-throated males begin showing juveniles to feeders by late June.

Jul.watchFor: Multiple hummingbirds competing at feeders. Young Pileated Woodpeckers begging from parents. Young Wild Turkeys with hens in clearing.

Aug.watchFor: Hummingbird activity peaks mid-August as birds fatten for migration. Early fall warblers passing through by late August. Broad-winged Hawks begin gathering.

Sep.watchFor: HIGHLIGHT: Sep 12–20 on NW wind after cold front — watch the sky from the clearing for Broad-winged Hawk kettles. Ruby-throated Hummingbird last sightings by late September.

Oct.watchFor: White-throated Sparrows return. Dark-eyed Juncos flock to feeders. Yellow-rumped Warblers moving through forest edges in large numbers.

Nov.watchFor: Cedar Waxwing flocks in fruiting trees (dogwood, holly). Hermit Thrush arrives.

Dec.watchFor: Barred Owls increasingly vocal. Pileated Woodpecker excavations visible in bare trees. Good time for owl listening on calm clear nights.

_meta.habitatContext: South-facing fairway clearing on a forested ridge at 2,959 ft, with mature mixed hardwood-pine forest on multiple sides, a pond, intermittent streams and seeps, and Lake Sequoyah at Tate Mountain Estates roughly 0.3 mi away. The mix of open clearing edge, mature forest interior, and nearby water concentrates a broad set of mid-Appalachian mammals — woodland edge species, forest interior species, and a smaller set of aquatic mammals working the lake.
_meta.notes: This is a curated property list, not a regional roster. Status framing reflects what Paul actually encounters: residents seen regularly, larger species known mainly from sign (tracks, scat, occasional sightings), and a small aquatic set tied to Lake Sequoyah. Activity windows are typical for mid-Appalachian elevations — variation by year is normal.

propertyHighlights.whyGoodMammalWatching: Church Mountain Road sits where a south-facing fairway clearing meets mature mixed forest, with the pond at the property and Lake Sequoyah just down the slope. That edge between open ground and deep woods is exactly where most southern Appalachian mammals do their daily work — deer browsing the clearing margins at dusk, foxes and coyotes hunting the edge after dark, raccoons and opossums working the woods at night. The lake adds the aquatic layer.
topFeatures: South-facing fairway edge: dawn and dusk movement for white-tailed deer, cottontails, and turkeys; foxes and coyotes hunt this margin after dark
Mature mixed hardwood-pine forest: gray squirrel, chipmunk, flying squirrel territory; bobcat and bear sign turns up in the forest interior
Property pond and seasonal seeps: drinking and foraging stops for nearly every mammal on this list
Lake Sequoyah at 0.3 mi: river otter and beaver work the lake itself, not the property
Bortle 3 dark sky: bats are visible against the night sky on summer evenings; flying squirrels glide silently between trees overhead

species.name: White-tailed Deer
species.habitat: Forest edges, clearings, mixed hardwood forest — heavy use of fairway margins at dawn and dusk
species.voice: Mostly silent. Snorts and blows when alarmed. Bucks grunt during the November rut; fawns bleat for does.
species.notes: The fairway clearing is exactly the kind of edge habitat white-tails work daily — they step out from the forest at dawn and dusk to browse along the margins, then drift back into cover. November is the rut at this elevation; bucks chase does across openings and rub young saplings to mark territory. Look for trails through the forest understory and scrapes in the leaf litter under low branches. Spotted fawns appear in May and June and lie hidden in deep grass while does feed nearby — leave them alone if you find one.
species.funFact: White-tails can clear an 8-foot fence from a standing start. The white-tail flag flashed when running is both an alarm signal to other deer and a 'follow me' cue for fawns.

species.name: Eastern Gray Squirrel
species.habitat: Mature mixed hardwood-pine forest, especially oak-hickory; uses the whole property
species.voice: Sharp chittering scolds and tail-flicking when alarmed. Soft 'kuk' calls between squirrels. Surprisingly loud for the size of the animal.
species.notes: The most constantly visible mammal on the property — gray squirrels work the oaks and hickories from first light through afternoon. Fall is peak activity: they spend October and November caching acorns and hickory nuts in shallow holes across the forest floor, most of which they'll relocate by smell through winter. The forgotten caches grow into the next generation of oaks. Listen for the rasping scrape of teeth on hickory shells at the base of trees in fall.
species.funFact: A single gray squirrel may cache several thousand nuts in a season and recover most of them by spatial memory and scent — the misses are a major mechanism of oak regeneration in eastern forests.

species.name: Eastern Chipmunk
species.statusLabel: Year-round resident (less active in deep winter)
species.habitat: Forest floor with stone walls, log piles, and downed wood; common at the forest-clearing edge
species.voice: Sharp, repeated 'chip-chip-chip' that can carry for surprising distances and continue for minutes. Lower 'chuck' notes when annoyed.
species.notes: Chipmunks work the forest floor in short, quick bursts — a flash of striped brown between the leaves and then nothing. The fairway edges and any stone walls or log piles on the property are prime denning territory. They retreat to underground burrows in the coldest weeks of winter but don't fully hibernate; on a mild January day you may still see one out briefly. Late summer through early fall is the busiest season as they stockpile seeds in their cheek pouches.
species.funFact: A chipmunk's cheek pouches can hold up to three times the size of its head in seeds. Burrow systems can run 20 to 30 feet underground with separate chambers for nesting, food storage, and waste.

species.name: Eastern Cottontail
species.habitat: Brushy edges, fairway clearing margins, thickets near cover
species.voice: Usually silent. A piercing, almost child-like scream when caught by a predator. Soft grunts between rabbits.
species.notes: Cottontails are at home along the fairway edge where short grass meets brushy cover — they feed in the open at dawn and dusk and stay within a few quick bounds of a thicket. Nests are shallow scrapes in the grass lined with fur and dry grass, hidden in plain sight; if you find a nest with young, leave it alone and check from a distance — the doe only returns at dawn and dusk to nurse. Predator pressure on this property is real: foxes, coyotes, bobcat, owls, and the occasional hawk all hunt rabbits.
species.funFact: A doe can have three to four litters per summer of four to five young each, and most cottontails do not survive their first year — the high reproductive rate is the species' answer to heavy predation.

species.name: Groundhog
species.habitat: Forest edges, clearings, slopes with well-drained soil for burrows
species.voice: Shrill whistle alarm call (the source of the name 'whistle-pig'). Teeth-chattering when threatened. Otherwise silent.
species.notes: Groundhogs are one of the few true hibernators on this list — they vanish into deep burrows around early November and don't reappear until late February or March, when males begin moving above ground to check territory. The fairway edges and well-drained slopes near the property are good burrow habitat. Look for the large entrance holes (6 to 10 inches across) with a fan of excavated dirt out front. They feed in mid-morning and late afternoon, sitting up periodically to scan for hawks and foxes.
species.funFact: Groundhog body temperature drops from about 99°F to under 40°F during hibernation, and the heart rate slows from about 80 beats per minute to four or five. They are the largest member of the squirrel family in this region.

species.name: Raccoon
species.habitat: Forest, forest edge, pond and stream margins, any structure with cavities
species.voice: An unusually wide vocal range — chittering, growling, hissing, whining, and the unmistakable high-pitched screams during mating season and territorial disputes. The screams sound startlingly like a person in trouble.
species.notes: Raccoons are a regular part of the night soundscape here. They work the property after dark — pond edges for crayfish and frogs, forest floor for grubs and acorns, anything they can pry open. The screaming and chittering that carries through the woods on humid summer nights is almost always raccoons sorting out territory or mates, not anything in distress. Tracks in soft mud near the pond show the unmistakable five-fingered handprint of the front paw. Females may den in tree cavities or under outbuildings to raise kits in May and June.
species.funFact: The Latin name *lotor* means 'washer' — the dipping-and-handling behavior that looks like washing is actually a way of using extremely sensitive paws to identify food by touch, and the wet paws are more sensitive than dry ones.

species.name: Virginia Opossum
species.habitat: Forest, forest edge, brush piles, any cover near food
species.voice: Mostly quiet. Hisses and growls when cornered, with the open-mouthed display showing 50 sharp teeth — the most of any North American land mammal. Young opossums make soft sneezing sounds.
species.notes: The opossum is the quiet half of the night-shift on this property — where raccoons announce themselves vocally, an opossum just trundles past in the headlights and disappears. They forage slowly along forest edges and any food source, eating almost anything: insects, grubs, fruit, carrion, ticks. North America's only marsupial. They don't truly play dead by choice — extreme stress triggers an involuntary catatonic state that can last minutes to hours, complete with foul-smelling secretions.
species.funFact: Opossums have remarkably low body temperatures (94–97°F) which makes them resistant to rabies — they almost never carry it. They also consume large numbers of ticks during grooming.

species.name: Striped Skunk
species.habitat: Forest edges, brush, pastures, any cover near food; dens in burrows, hollow logs, under outbuildings
species.voice: Mostly silent. Foot-stomping and tail-raising as warning displays before spraying. Soft growls and whines.
species.notes: Skunks are nocturnal and methodical — they work the forest edge and clearing margins at night, digging shallow conical holes for grubs and insects. February is breeding season and you may smell skunk on the air on calm winter nights well before you see one. The strong, distinctive scent on the wind is often the only sign one passed through. Striped skunks give plenty of warning before spraying (stomping, hissing, tail-up display); a slow retreat is the right response.
species.funFact: Skunks can spray up to about 10 feet with reasonable accuracy. Great horned owls are one of the few predators that regularly take skunks — owls have a poor sense of smell.

species.name: Red Fox
species.habitat: Forest edges, clearings, open ground with cover; prefers more open habitat than the gray fox
species.voice: A wide vocal repertoire including yips, barks, and a startling raspy scream sometimes heard on winter nights during the January–February breeding season.
species.notes: Red foxes use more open habitat than gray foxes — the fairway clearing margins are exactly where you might see one trotting at dawn or dusk. They hunt small mammals by sound, leaping in a high arc and pinning prey through snow or deep grass with the front paws. Winter is the most vocal season as breeding pairs establish territory; the scream is unsettling the first time you hear it. Kits emerge from natal dens in April and May, and family groups may be visible briefly in early summer.
species.funFact: Red foxes use the earth's magnetic field to calibrate hunting leaps — studies show they're more successful when pouncing toward the northeast, which suggests they line up prey by sound and magnetic bearing simultaneously.

species.name: Gray Fox
species.statusLabel: Year-round resident (more nocturnal than red fox)
species.habitat: Mature mixed hardwood forest, brushy edges, slopes with cover; prefers more closed forest than the red fox
species.voice: Yips, sharp barks, and a hoarse rasping cry during the January–February breeding season. Quieter overall than red fox.
species.notes: Gray foxes are the more forest-loving of the two foxes here — they prefer the closed mixed hardwood interior and brushy edges over the open fairway. They are the only canid in North America that climbs trees, using semi-retractable claws to escape predators or hunt nesting birds. More nocturnal than red foxes, so encounters are rare; tracks and scat (often deposited on prominent stumps or rocks as scent marks) are easier to find than the fox itself. The black-tipped tail and salt-and-pepper gray back distinguish them from red fox.
species.funFact: The gray fox is the only member of the dog family in the Western Hemisphere that routinely climbs trees, and one of only two canids worldwide with this ability. It can climb branchless vertical trunks to more than 50 feet.

species.name: Coyote
species.habitat: Forest, forest edge, clearings — uses nearly all habitat types on the property
species.voice: Highly vocal — yips, barks, and the group yip-howl that can make two or three coyotes sound like a dozen. Most vocal in fall as pups learn to howl and in winter during the breeding season.
species.notes: Coyotes are well-established across the Blue Ridge — every county in Georgia has them now, and the forested ridges around Church Mountain Road are typical habitat. They hunt mostly at night, working forest edges and clearings for rabbits, small mammals, fawns, and carrion. The group yip-howl is one of the most striking sounds of an Appalachian night — a family group's chorus can carry for miles on a calm evening. Fall is the most vocal season as that year's pups practice howling alongside adults.
species.funFact: Eastern coyotes are slightly larger than their western counterparts because of historical hybridization with wolves as the species expanded eastward across the Great Lakes region — they carry a small but measurable percentage of wolf and dog DNA.

species.name: Black Bear
species.habitat: Large blocks of mature forest with mast (acorns, hickory nuts, berries); a wide-ranging species, not pinned to any single spot
species.voice: Mostly silent. Huffs, jaw-pops, and tongue-clicks as warnings. Cubs make sharp 'whimpering' calls. Adults can produce moaning and bellowing during stress or near food.
species.notes: Black bears are part of the Blue Ridge but rarely seen on any single property — their home ranges are large and they move widely with the seasons. On this property the signs are what to watch for: claw-marked trees, overturned logs, scat full of berry seeds or acorn hulls, and the distinctive 'bear-trail' where a bear has stepped repeatedly in the same depressions over months or years. Spring (April–May) and fall (August–October) are the most active seasons; bears den from late November through February. Keep trash secured and bird feeders pulled in April through November to avoid drawing them close to buildings.
species.funFact: Black bears don't truly hibernate — they enter a state called torpor where body temperature drops only slightly and they can wake quickly if disturbed. Females give birth in the den in January and nurse cubs through the winter while fasting.

species.name: Bobcat
species.habitat: Mixed forest with dense cover and early successional edges; uses 5–10+ square miles of home range
species.voice: Usually silent. During the winter breeding season, produces hair-raising yowls, screams, and caterwauling that can sound deeply alarming the first time you hear one.
species.notes: Bobcats are the most elusive resident on this list — present but rarely glimpsed. They are crepuscular, moving most at dawn and dusk, and a single bobcat may patrol a home range of 5 to 10 square miles, which means any one stretch of forest sees them only occasionally. Signs are what to look for: round, claw-less tracks (about 2 inches across), scat on prominent rocks or stumps, and scrapes in the leaf litter at territorial markers. The winter breeding season (January–February) produces the most likely chance to hear one — the screams carry far on cold nights.
species.funFact: Bobcats can leap horizontally up to 12 feet to take down prey. Their retractable claws don't show in tracks, which is one of the cleanest ways to distinguish bobcat tracks from those of a dog or coyote.

species.name: North American River Otter
species.habitat: Lake Sequoyah and connected waterways — not the property itself, but the lake at 0.3 mi
species.voice: Whistles, chirps, and growls between family members. A sharp 'huff' alarm call. Generally not loud, but social and vocal when together.
species.notes: River otters are present in Georgia waters throughout the state and are at home in the kind of lake-edge-with-cover habitat that Lake Sequoyah provides. They are unusual among water mammals in being mostly diurnal — daytime visits to the lake shore are the best chance of an encounter. Look for slide marks on muddy banks where they enter and exit the water, and for piles of crayfish shells (their summer staple in Georgia) at favorite latrines. Otters often den in abandoned beaver lodges, so the two species often share the same water.
species.funFact: An otter can hold its breath underwater for up to 8 minutes and close its ears and nostrils against water entry. The dense fur is up to a million hairs per square inch — the densest fur of any mammal.

species.name: American Beaver
species.habitat: Lake Sequoyah edges and connected streams — not the property pond
species.voice: Mostly silent. The dramatic tail-slap on water as an alarm signal is more often heard than any vocalization. Soft mewing between family members at the lodge.
species.notes: Beavers are well-established across the southern Appalachians and the Lake Sequoyah area provides the slow water and woody vegetation they need. They are largely nocturnal — dawn and dusk visits to the lake are the best opportunity to see one. Look for the unmistakable signs: gnawed stumps with their characteristic pencil-pointed cone, peeled sticks and branches at the water's edge, and well-worn slides between water and the nearest hardwoods. The startling crack of a tail-slap on the lake surface is an alarm signal and a reliable announcement that you are being noticed.
species.funFact: Beavers are the second-largest rodent in the world after the capybara. Their continuously-growing incisors are reinforced with iron, giving them their distinctive orange color and the hardness needed to fell hardwood trees.

species.name: Southern Flying Squirrel
species.habitat: Mature hardwood and mixed forest with nesting cavities — uses the whole forested portion of the property
species.voice: High-pitched chirps, trills, and bird-like whistles, much of it ultrasonic and inaudible to humans. The audible portion sounds more like a small bird than a squirrel.
species.notes: Flying squirrels are likely more common on this property than the daytime gray squirrels — they're simply invisible because they are strictly nocturnal. They glide between trees rather than fly, using a furred membrane (the patagium) stretched between front and back legs to cover up to 150 feet between launches. The Bortle 3 dark sky makes silhouette spotting more practical here than in most places: on warm humid summer nights, watch the night sky between large trees from the fairway edge. A red flashlight beam (which they don't react to) on a known den tree is the most reliable way to see one.
species.funFact: Most southern flying squirrel vocalizations are ultrasonic, above the range of human hearing. Their large dark eyes — proportionally enormous — gather every available scrap of starlight for night gliding.

species.name: Bats
species.habitat: Aerial — foraging over the fairway clearing, pond, and forest canopy edge at dusk
species.voice: Echolocation calls are ultrasonic and inaudible to humans without a bat detector. The audible sound at a property is the soft flutter of wings and the occasional faint chitter near roost sites.
species.notes: Bats are reliably present here in warm months but the specific species mix is not confirmed on the property. North Georgia hosts a number of species — big brown bat, eastern red bat, hoary bat, tri-colored bat, and several others — and the most likely visitors at this elevation and habitat are generalists working the airspace over the clearing and pond at dusk. The Bortle 3 dark sky makes them easier to spot than most places: stand at the fairway edge in the first 30 minutes after sunset between May and August, and watch the airspace 10 to 50 feet up for fluttering silhouettes against the still-lit sky. White-nose syndrome has devastated cave-hibernating species across the Southeast since 2010 — any healthy bat population here matters.
species.funFact: A single bat may eat 600–1,000 mosquito-sized insects in an hour. To identify species at a property usually requires either a bat detector (which translates ultrasonic calls into audible frequencies) or careful daytime photos of roosting individuals.

highlights: Coyote and fox breeding — most vocal nights of the year
Bobcat breeding season — possible screams on cold still nights
Bears in den; groundhogs in true hibernation
Gray squirrels visible against bare trees
Jan.watchFor: Calm cold nights are prime listening time — coyote yip-howls, fox screams, occasional bobcat caterwauls. Most other mammals are quiet or denned.

highlights: Skunk breeding — distinctive scent on the air at night
Foxes continuing to breed and mark territory
First groundhog emergence by late month
Feb.watchFor: Sheds appear on deer trails through the forest understory. Skunks are more active than any other month — drive carefully at dusk.
